PROP
42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Prohibits any new state tax (1) imposed on the ownership of personal property (all things people own other than real estate), or (2) that applies retroactively based on taxpayer’s past activities. Nullifies taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that conflict with this measure. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future. Supporters: CA Professional Firefighters; State Building & Construction Trades Council of CA; AMVETS Department of CA Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
California’s Constitution currently allows the Legislature to tax retirement and savings—even though you already paid taxes on that money when you earned it! Prop. 42 protects Californians from this double taxation, by prohibiting new and retroactive taxes on personal property, including retirement and savings. You earned it. Prop. 42 protects it.
CON
This is just another billionaire-funded trick. Prop. 42 isn’t really about protecting your retirement savings—its only real purpose is to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Vote NO on 42.

California Statewide Direct Primary Election Tuesday, June 3, 2014
## Official Voter Information Guide

## PUBLIC RECORDS. OPEN MEETINGS. STATE REIMBURSEMENT TO LOCAL AGENCIES. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
## ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
...
### PROPOSAL
This measure:
- Adds to the State Constitution the requirement that local governments follow the Public Records Act and the Brown Act.
- Eliminates the state's responsibility to pay local governments for their costs related to these laws.
(As noted above, state responsibility to pay for local Brown Act costs was eliminated in 2012.)
The measure applies to the current requirements of these laws, as well as any future changes to either law that are made to improve public access to government information or meetings.
### FISCAL EFFECTS
***Effect on State Costs and Local Revenues.*** By eliminating the state's responsibility for paying local government costs to follow the Public Records Act, the measure would result in savings to the state and comparable revenue reductions to local governments.
The impact is likely in the tens of millions of dollars a year.

## California Secretary of State Shirley N. Weber, Ph.D., Announces the Statewide Voter Information Guide for the November 3, 2026, General Election Is Available for Public Review
**Sacramento, Calif.** – Today California Secretary of State Shirley N. Weber, Ph.D., made the November 3, 2026, California General Election Official Voter Information Guide available for public review.
The guide, which will be mailed to every voting household in California, includes information about propositions and statements from candidates running for constitutional offices, as well as other important election information such as the California Voter Bill of Rights and information about how eligible Californians can vote.
California’s Official Voter Information Guide is available in 10 languages—English, Spanish, Chinese, Hindi, Japanese, Khmer, Korean, Tagalog, Thai, and Vietnamese.
The guide is available for public examination from July 21, 2026 through August 10, 2026 at https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/public-display and at the Office of the Secretary of State’s Sacramento and Los Angeles locations.
...
Following the conclusion of the public examination period, the Office of the Secretary of State will begin printing and mailing the statewide Voter Information Guide to all households that have at least one registered voter.

PROP
42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Prohibits any new state tax (1) imposed on the ownership of personal property (all things people own other than real estate), or (2) that applies retroactively based on taxpayer’s past activities. Nullifies taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that conflict with this measure. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future. Supporters: CA Professional Firefighters; State Building & Construction Trades Council of CA; AMVETS Department of CA Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
California’s Constitution currently allows the Legislature to tax retirement and savings—even though you already paid taxes on that money when you earned it! Prop. 42 protects Californians from this double taxation, by prohibiting new and retroactive taxes on personal property, including retirement and savings. You earned it. Prop. 42 protects it.
CON
This is just another billionaire-funded trick. Prop. 42 isn’t really about protecting your retirement savings—its only real purpose is to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Vote NO on 42.

## ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
...
### PROPOSAL
This measure:
- Adds to the State Constitution the requirement that local governments follow the Public Records Act and the Brown Act.
- Eliminates the state's responsibility to pay local governments for their costs related to these laws.
(As noted above, state responsibility to pay for local Brown Act costs was eliminated in 2012.)
The measure applies to the current requirements of these laws, as well as any future changes to either law that are made to improve public access to government information or meetings.
### FISCAL EFFECTS
***Effect on State Costs and Local Revenues.*** By eliminating the state's responsibility for paying local government costs to follow the Public Records Act, the measure would result in savings to the state and comparable revenue reductions to local governments.
The impact is likely in the tens of millions of dollars a year.

## California Secretary of State Shirley N. Weber, Ph.D., Announces the Statewide Voter Information Guide for the November 3, 2026, General Election Is Available for Public Review
**Sacramento, Calif.** – Today California Secretary of State Shirley N. Weber, Ph.D., made the November 3, 2026, California General Election Official Voter Information Guide available for public review.
The guide, which will be mailed to every voting household in California, includes information about propositions and statements from candidates running for constitutional offices, as well as other important election information such as the California Voter Bill of Rights and information about how eligible Californians can vote.
California’s Official Voter Information Guide is available in 10 languages—English, Spanish, Chinese, Hindi, Japanese, Khmer, Korean, Tagalog, Thai, and Vietnamese.
The guide is available for public examination from July 21, 2026 through August 10, 2026 at https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/public-display and at the Office of the Secretary of State’s Sacramento and Los Angeles locations.

42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Prohibits any new state tax (1) imposed on the ownership of personal property (all things people own other than real estate), or (2) that applies retroactively based on taxpayer’s past activities. Nullifies taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that conflict with this measure. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future. Supporters: CA Professional Firefighters; State Building & Construction Trades Council of CA; AMVETS Department of CA Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
California’s Constitution currently allows the Legislature to tax retirement and savings—even though you already paid taxes on that money when you earned it! Prop. 42 protects Californians from this double taxation, by prohibiting new and retroactive taxes on personal property, including retirement and savings. You earned it. Prop. 42 protects it.
CON
This is just another billionaire-funded trick. Prop. 42 isn’t really about protecting your retirement savings—its only real purpose is to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Vote NO on 42.

Wait, re-read: "Proposition 42 — Property and retroactive taxes: Prohibits new state personal property taxes and retroactive tax legislation. Kalshi: 79% | Polymarket: 80%". Hmm, that article says bettors expect Prop 42 to pass at ~80%. But the defirate page observed Nov 2-3: "Prop 42: 56% chance to pass (Kalshi 57%, Polymarket 54%)" — "close to a coin flip," "Lean pass". The nijinn.io aggregator: Polymarket for the compound market "Prop 40 defeats Props 41 and 42" at 7.4%.

So the most current prediction market data (Nov 2-3): Prop 42 chance to pass ~54-57%. That's a lean toward Yes passing, but close.

Key considerations:
- Late-deciding voters historically break "no" on initiatives. IGS Director DiCamillo: "It's below 50%, and it's trending down. Both of those are ominous signs" for Prop 42. "still very close... it's moving in the wrong direction late in the campaign."
- Money: Yes side $128M vs No side $22.7M. Yes has huge spending advantage. But the anti side's message ("billionaire trick") has been effective, opposition rising.
- Partisan split: Republicans 74% yes, independents 61% yes, Democrats 39% yes (Sept PPIC). By October, "most Democrats would vote no."
- Newsom endorsed Prop 42 (Yes).

The prediction markets as of Nov 2-3 give Yes ~54-57% — lean pass. The defirate summary says "Prop 42 is close to a coin flip," "Lean pass."

Hmm, but note the Yahoo article earlier says Kalshi 79% / Polymarket 80% for Prop 42 — that might be from mid/late October. The market moved down toward 54-57% by Nov 2-3. So markets lean Yes but barely.

Two most recent polls: PPIC Oct 16-22: Yes 51-47 (Yes +4). IGS Oct 19-25: No 45-43 (No +2). Average: essentially tied, slight edge... 51+43=94 yes vs 47+45=92 no across the two polls. Basically even.

Historical California ballot measure behavior: measures polling below 50% yes typically fail because undecideds break no. In the IGS poll, yes is 43%, no 45%, undecided 12%. If undecideds break no, it fails. In PPIC, yes 51%, no 47%, 2% undecided — PPIC's likely voter model has few undecideds.

The markets currently price ~55% yes. Given the question demands a binary answer, I should go with the market-implied favorite but weigh the trend.

Let me think more about the dynamics:
- Prop 40 (wealth tax) is likely to fail (~25% chance per markets). 
- For Prop 42: supporters spent $128M. The No campaign spent $22.7M but their message was amplified by the fight over Prop 40.
- The IGS trend for Prop 42: 43-34 (Sept) → 43-45 (Oct). Yes flat at 43, No rose 11 points. Undecided fell from 23 to 12. If that trend continues into the final week, No keeps gaining. Remaining 12% undecided historically break heavily no. That suggests final result could be something like 45-55 No. But PPIC shows yes hanging on at 51-47.

- Confusion factor: Props 40, 41, 42 are interlinked and confusing. Confused voters vote no. That cuts against 42.

- On the other hand: the "yes" argument (protect retirement savings from taxes) is intuitively appealing, and the ballot label "Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes" sounds good to low-information voters. PPIC asks with the official label and gets 51% yes. IGS shows a different result. Note IGS shows ballot label too presumably.

- Partisan: CA is heavily Democratic; Democratic Party and Bernie Sanders oppose; but Newsom (very popular Dem governor) supports. Labor is split: firefighters/building trades for; SEIU against.

Market odds are the strongest single predictor: ~54-57% yes as of Nov 2-3. But there's an important nuance: the market at nijinn (Polymarket only) for the compound "Prop 40 defeats Props 41 and 42" is 7.4%, not directly relevant.

Actually, the numbers I have: defirate observed Nov 2, 10:07 PM ET – Nov 3, 4:05 AM ET: Prop 42 chance to pass 56% (Kalshi 57%, Polymarket 54%). "Lean pass."

Hmm, wait — one defirate line says "Prop 42 is close to a coin flip... Closest measure 56% Yes About 3 in 5" and table says 56% (Kalshi 57%, Poly 54%). Also there was a line "Kalshi59¢ Polymarket Poly92¢" — confusing, but the table is clear: ~54-57%.

The Yahoo article (undated but seems ~Oct 29-30): Kalshi 79% | Polymarket 80% for Prop 42. Hmm, that's a big discrepancy with defirate's Nov 2-3 observation of 54-57%. A drop from 80% to 56%? Possible if the Berkeley IGS poll (No +2) moved markets. Actually the Berkeley poll came out Oct 29. Hmm, but would that drop it 25 points? The IGS poll showed yes stuck at 43 and no rising to 45. Markets may have overreacted... or the Yahoo numbers were stale.

Either way, the most current market read (Nov 2-3) is ~55% yes — a slight lean to Yes passing.

Now, which is more likely? Let me weigh:

Arguments for Yes (passing):
1. Prediction markets lean yes (~55%).
2. Massive spending advantage ($128M vs $23M), and yes ads framing as "protect your retirement."
3. PPIC (most recent, Oct 16-22, n=1,086 LV) still shows yes ahead 51-47.
4. Newsom endorsement; intuitive appeal of the ballot title; Republican + independent support strong.
5. Prop 40 failing badly might reduce turnout motivation of anti-42 voters; also some voters may vote yes on 42 as insurance.

Arguments for No (failing):
1. Trend: opposition rising, yes support flat/declining; late movement usually continues.
2. Undecideds historically break no; IGS has yes at 43% — well below 50. DiCamillo (top CA pollster) calls the signs "ominous."
3. IGS (most recent, Oct 19-25) shows No ahead 45-43.
4. Democratic Party opposition in a blue state; "billionaire trick" framing effective; confusion across three measures → vote no on all.
5. CA initiatives polling below 50% pre-election usually fail.

This is genuinely close — a near coin flip. The question forces a binary answer. Prediction markets are generally the best calibrated single source, and they lean slightly yes (54-57%). But polling trend and CA ballot measure history lean no.

How to read California proposition odds
A Yes contract pays $1 if the measure passes and nothing if it fails, so a price of 70¢ is a 70% chance. The average column is the mean of the venues that list the measure. Most proposition markets are thin: little money has traded, and the gap between the price to buy and the price to sell can be wide, so a single trade can move them. Prop 40, the billionaire tax, is the exception, with by far the most trading and its own markets on the margin of victory and on whether the tax takes effect.

5. Prop 40 failing badly might reduce turnout motivation of anti-42 voters; also some voters may vote yes on 42 as insurance.

Arguments for No (failing):
1. Trend: opposition rising, yes support flat/declining; late movement usually continues.
2. Undecideds historically break no; IGS has yes at 43% — well below 50. DiCamillo (top CA pollster) calls the signs "ominous."
3. IGS (most recent, Oct 19-25) shows No ahead 45-43.
4. Democratic Party opposition in a blue state; "billionaire trick" framing effective; confusion across three measures → vote no on all.
5. CA initiatives polling below 50% pre-election usually fail.

This is genuinely close — a near coin flip. The question forces a binary answer. Prediction markets are generally the best calibrated single source, and they lean slightly yes (54-57%). But polling trend and CA ballot measure history lean no.

Also worth checking: does the question come from a specific prediction market framing? "Which side is more likely to win?" with the voterguide link — it's likely from a market asking "Will Proposition 42 pass?" Yes = passes. Given markets lean ~55% yes at the last observation... but the momentum is clearly toward no.

How to read California proposition odds
A Yes contract pays $1 if the measure passes and nothing if it fails, so a price of 70¢ is a 70% chance. The average column is the mean of the venues that list the measure. Most proposition markets are thin: little money has traded, and the gap between the price to buy and the price to sell can be wide, so a single trade can move them. Prop 40, the billionaire tax, is the exception, with by far the most trading and its own markets on the margin of victory and on whether the tax takes effect.

# Newsom’s poison-pill problem
Prop 42 — funded by wealth tax opponents like Google co-founder **Sergey Brin** and endorsed by Newsom — contains a poison pill provision that would void Prop 40’s one-time 5% tax on billionaires’ assets.
If both measures pass, whichever receives the most yes votes goes into effect.
That’s not the likeliest outcome, but also not impossible.
One recent PPIC poll shows Prop 42 passing with 54% of the vote, and Prop 40 eking by with 52%.
And it’s not hard to imagine the far-reaching uproar if voters approve a billionaires tax, only to be overruled by a billionaire-backed measure pitched as a protection for retirement savings.
...

PROP
42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Prohibits any new state tax (1) imposed on the ownership of personal property (all things people own other than real estate), or (2) that applies retroactively based on taxpayer’s past activities. Nullifies taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that conflict with this measure. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future. Supporters: CA Professional Firefighters; State Building & Construction Trades Council of CA; AMVETS Department of CA Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
California’s Constitution currently allows the Legislature to tax retirement and savings—even though you already paid taxes on that money when you earned it! Prop. 42 protects Californians from this double taxation, by prohibiting new and retroactive taxes on personal property, including retirement and savings. You earned it. Prop. 42 protects it.
CON
This is just another billionaire-funded trick. Prop. 42 isn’t really about protecting your retirement savings—its only real purpose is to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Vote NO on 42.

...
### PROPOSAL
This measure:
- Adds to the State Constitution the requirement that local governments follow the Public Records Act and the Brown Act.
- Eliminates the state's responsibility to pay local governments for their costs related to these laws.
(As noted above, state responsibility to pay for local Brown Act costs was eliminated in 2012.)
The measure applies to the current requirements of these laws, as well as any future changes to either law that are made to improve public access to government information or meetings.
### FISCAL EFFECTS
***Effect on State Costs and Local Revenues.*** By eliminating the state's responsibility for paying local government costs to follow the Public Records Act, the measure would result in savings to the state and comparable revenue reductions to local governments.
The impact is likely in the tens of millions of dollars a year.

Prop.
42 amends the California Constitution by adding Article VIII, Sections 1 through 9.
Under Proposition 42, new taxes on the ownership of financial assets (e.g. pensions, stocks, or retirement accounts) and tangible or intangible personal property would not be allowed.
Proposition 42 also prohibits retroactive taxes that authorize a tax on conduct, activities, or status that occurred or was present prior to the effective date of the state law or constitution.

Prediction markets as of Nov 2-3, 2026 (Election Day is Nov 3):
- Kalshi: Prop 42 passes — 57% (Yes 58¢ bid, per Kalshi page; "▼ 5" indicating a 5-point drop recently)

- Berkeley IGS Oct 19-25: Yes 43, No 45 (No +2)
- Trend: opposition rising, support declining; undecideds breaking no; but PPIC still shows yes majority with few undecideds.

Fundamentals:
- Yes side: $128M (vs $23M), Newsom endorsement, favorable ballot label, strong R/I support.
- No side: rising momentum, CA Dem Party opposition, undecided-break-no dynamic, confusion among Props 40/41/42.

The question: "Which side is more likely to win? Answer with only yes or no."

Given the market consensus (~55-57% yes), the money advantage, and PPIC's final poll showing yes ahead — versus the negative momentum and IGS showing no ahead — this is close to a coin flip but the balance of evidence tilts slightly toward Yes passing:
- Two independent markets (Kalshi 57%, Polymarket 54%) both price yes above 50% with real money.
- The best-regarded CA pollster (PPIC) shows yes ahead 51-47 with only 2% undecided.
- 5.6:1 spending advantage with closing ad blitz.
- Kalshi's related market (Prop 42 gets more yes votes than Prop 40) at 70% implies traders expect strong yes numbers for 42.

Countervailing: IGS trend and the undecided-break-no pattern suggest no. DiCamillo's "ominous signs" comment.

Overall probability of Yes: I'd estimate ~53-57%. Slightly above 50%. So the answer to "Which side is more likely to win?" → the Yes side → answer "yes."

Hmm, but let me double-check my instinct against the "undecideds break no" rule. In the PPIC poll, only 2% undecided — so the undecided-break-no effect is largely already priced in there, and yes still leads 51-47. IGS with 12% undecided shows no +2 — if undecideds break 2:1 no, final would be ~47-53 no. The two pollsters disagree meaningfully (house effects in likely-voter modeling). Markets split the difference and lean yes slightly.

Money matters in CA ballot fights — the side with 5.6x spending advantage in the final two weeks usually moves numbers. The no side's momentum occurred despite being massively outspent, which is notable, but the yes side's saturation advertising in the final week (plus Newsom's endorsement amplified in ads) may stabilize yes.

Also consider base rates: since 2000, California initiatives leading in the final PPIC poll pass a large majority of the time. Prop 42 leads in the final PPIC poll.

I'll go with "yes" — the Yes side is slightly more likely to win. The market consensus is the tiebreaker, and it consistently (Kalshi 56-57%, Polymarket 54%) leans yes.

Actually, wait. Let me be careful about one thing: the Kalshi page snippet says "57% ▼ 5 — Yes 58¢ No 43¢" — the ▼5 means it dropped 5 points recently, consistent with late momentum toward no. And Polymarket at 54%. Average ~55%. Markets still lean yes.

Final answer: yes.

Based on my research, here's the picture for **California Proposition 42** (Nov. 3, 2026 — the measure to prohibit new state personal property/wealth taxes and retroactive taxes, backed by Sergey Brin and endorsed by Gov. Newsom, opposed by Bernie Sanders/SEIU):

**Polling (final):**
- PPIC (Oct 16–22): **Yes 51%, No 47%** — Yes ahead with only 2% undecided
- Berkeley IGS (Oct 19–25): **No 45%, Yes 43%** — No ahead, with opposition rising fast (from 34% in Sept)
- Clear negative momentum for the Yes side; undecideds have been breaking No

**Prediction markets (as of Nov 2–3):**
- Kalshi: ~57% chance Prop 42 passes
- Polymarket: ~54% chance it passes
- Kalshi's related market: 70% chance Prop 42 gets more yes votes than Prop 40

**Fundamentals:**
- Yes side outspent No roughly $128M to $23M (~5.6:1), with a favorable ballot title ("Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes"), Newsom's endorsement, and strong Republican/independent support
- No side had momentum, the "billionaire trick" framing, and Democratic Party opposition

Weighing it all: it's near a coin flip, but real-money markets on two venues both price the Yes side above 50%, the most trusted California pollster (PPIC) has Yes ahead with almost no undecideds left, and the Yes side's massive spending advantage and favorable label favor it in the final days.

**yes**
